column1: # Known divergences between IDL front ends.
# `spikes/differential.sh` fails on any file where the oracles disagree with
# each other, because such a file does not mean the same thing to every
# deployed compiler. Some of those disagreements are real and permanent: a
# compiler is lax where the specification is strict, or cannot resolve
# something the specification requires. Those belong here, with the reason we
# side with one oracle over the other.
# An entry is an exemption from failing, never from being reported. A recorded
# divergence that stops happening is also flagged — an exemption that no longer
# describes reality is worse than none, because it silently covers whatever
# takes its place.
# Columns: file <TAB> oracle <TAB> that oracle's verdict <TAB> why we accept it
# One value in the oracle column is not a compiler: `spec` records a place where
# a deployed compiler and the published specification disagree, rather than two
# compilers disagreeing with each other. `differential.sh` never runs an oracle
# by that name, so such a row is inert there — it does not exempt anything and
# is not reported stale. It is here because it is the same kind of finding and
# belongs in the same file, and because the verdict is the same either way:
# interop is with deployed compilers, not with a document.
# `spec`은 컴파일러가 아니라 규격 문언과 배포 컴파일러가 갈리는 지점을 기록하는
# 값이다. differential.sh는 그 이름의 오라클을 실행하지 않으므로 면제도 아니고
# 미발생 경고도 뜨지 않는다. 상호운용 대상은 문서가 아니라 배포된 컴파일러다.
# 파일별 알려진 오라클 불일치. 규격이 엄격한 곳에서 특정 컴파일러가 느슨한 경우처럼
# 실재하고 영구적인 불일치를 사유와 함께 기록한다. 등록은 실패 면제일 뿐 보고 면제가
# 아니며, 더 이상 발생하지 않는 등록도 함께 지적된다.
# ── Divergences that are NOT rows here ──────────────────────────────────────
# `corpus/include/` holds the multi-file cases, and `differential.sh` does not
# examine that directory — it enumerates golden, negative, requirements and
# spikes by name, and half of `corpus/include/` is leaf files that mean nothing
# on their own. A row here for a file it never runs would be reported as a
# stale exemption on every single run, so the two deliberate divergences that
# directory carries live in `corpus/include/cases.tsv` beside the files they
# describe, with the same columns and the same obligation to state a reason.
# They point in opposite directions and both are named there:
#   service.idl      we ACCEPT what omniidl rejects  (unguarded double include)
#   conditional.idl  we REFUSE what omniidl compiles (conditional compilation)
# `corpus/include/`의 다중 파일 케이스는 `differential.sh`가 검사하지 않으므로
# 여기에 행을 두면 매 실행마다 "더 이상 발생하지 않는 등록"으로 보고된다. 그
# 두 건의 의도적 불일치는 파일 옆 `corpus/include/cases.tsv`에 같은 의무로
# 기록되어 있다 — 한 건은 우리가 더 느슨하고, 한 건은 더 엄격하다.
n02-identifier-clash.idl
column4: CORBA 3.4 §7.2.3 makes identifier collisions case-insensitive, so `Position position` is illegal. omniidl rejects it; JacORB 3.9 does not enforce the rule at all. We follow the specification and omniidl. This is the project's dominant generation failure, and finding that a widely deployed compiler accepts it is a reason to be stricter, not looser: IDL that builds under JacORB can fail under omniORB.

column1: n10-operation-name-clash.idl
column4: The same rule in its operation-name shape (`Blob blob()`). JacORB 3.9 does not enforce it; omniidl does. Same verdict, same reason.

column1: n12-enum-member-case-clash.idl
column4: The same non-enforcement (n02, n10), in the shape it took in a real external document: docs/CORBAMoEArchitecture.md §7 wrote `Residency residency`, and JacORB 3.9 would have built it while omniidl and our front end refuse. That is the divergence's danger stated as a case, not a hypothesis — same verdict, same reason. (Its sibling defect n11, `struct Context`, diverges nowhere: JacORB does reject keyword collisions.)

column1: 12-any-typecode.idl
column4: JacORB 3.9 cannot resolve the fully-qualified `::CORBA::TypeCode`; it reports `Undefined name: gc12.Bag.CORBA.TypeCode`, having looked the absolute scope up relative to the enclosing one. omniidl resolves it, and CLAUDE.md requires the qualified spelling because the unqualified one is itself a case clash. The file stays as written.

column1: p02-prefix-inside-module.idl
column4: CORBA 3.4 §14.7.5.1 describes `#pragma prefix` as a prefix: the string is inserted between `IDL:` and the scoped name, which reads as `IDL:acme.com/p02/Ledger:1.0`. omniidl 4.3.4 instead *replaces* the accumulated scope path with the pragma's string, dropping the enclosing module: measured `IDL:acme.com/Ledger:1.0` on 2026-08-14 via `omniidl -bpython`. At file scope the two readings coincide, which is why the difference stays hidden until a real file puts the pragma inside a module. We follow omniidl — a repository id is identity on the wire, and being right about a document while disagreeing with the ORB on the other end is the failure this batch exists to close.

column1: p05-prefix-does-not-escape.idl
column4: The same divergence in the shape that also pins the scoping rule: `p05a::Inside`, declared after a prefix pragma inside `module p05a`, is `IDL:inner.example/Inside:1.0` and not `IDL:inner.example/p05a/Inside:1.0`. The rest of the file measures what both readings agree on — the prefix does not survive the closing brace, so `p05b::Outside` is plain `IDL:p05b/Outside:1.0`.

column1: 30-const-type.idl
column4: CORBA 3.4 §7.4.1.4.2's `const_type` admits `fixed_pt_const_type ::= "fixed"` — a fixed-point constant whose digits and scale come from its value, with no `<d,s>`. omniidl 4.3.4 accepts it and folds `CEILING - 0.01d`; JacORB 3.9's lexer refuses the bare keyword (`line: 32(46): Syntax error … Couldn't repair and continue parse`, measured 2026-08-20). We side with omniidl and the grammar: the file exists to pin the production, and the shape JacORB accepts — `const fixed<3,1>` — is the one omniidl calls a syntax error and `corpus/negative/n18` pins as rejected.

column1: 31-native-type.idl
column4: CORBA 3.4 §7.4.4 makes `native <identifier>;` a declaration every front end must parse, and JacORB 3.9 does parse it — a file containing nothing but `native Handle;` compiles clean. It falls over on the first *use*: `struct S { Handle t; };` produces a NullPointerException, not a diagnostic (`Cannot invoke "org.jacorb.idl.TypeDeclaration.getTypeCodeExpression()" because "this.type_decl" is null`, measured 2026-08-21). omniidl accepts the whole file; its C++ back end exits 1 on the declaration alone and its Python back end ignores it. We side with omniidl and the grammar: the file exists to pin that a `native` parses and has no wire form, and a crash is not a rejection — the third front end simply has no representation for a type it cannot marshal, which is the finding this file was written to record.

column1: 32-valuebase.idl
column4: `ValueBase` is the keyword for the abstract base of every valuetype (CORBA 3.4 §7.4.1.4). omniidl resolves it, dumps it as `::CORBA::ValueBase`, and writes it as `tk_value` — 72 bytes, VM_NONE, no concrete base, no members, measured 2026-08-21. JacORB 3.9 answers `struct E { ValueBase p; };` with a NullPointerException (`Cannot invoke "org.jacorb.idl.BaseType.getTCKind()" because "this.type_spec" is null`) rather than a diagnostic. Same verdict and the same reason as the row above: we follow omniidl, and a crash is not a rejection.

column1: 33-const-values.idl
column4: JacORB 3.9 cannot lex a `fixed` literal whose integer part is written and starts with `0`. `0.0d`, `0.5d`, `0.001d`, `0.10d`, `00.0d`, `0d` and `000000001d` each stop the parse at the literal ("Syntax error", then "Couldn't repair and continue parse"), while the identical values are taken with the integer part absent (`.5d`), with a sign in front (`-0.5d`, `-0.001d`), and whenever the first integer digit is nonzero (`1.0d`, `1.00d`, `2.50d`, `100d`). It is specific to the `d` suffix and not to the leading zero: `const double B = 0.0;` and `const long C = 010;` both compile. Measured 2026-08-24, twenty-one one-line probes, after the machine that produced this file had no second front end to ask. omniidl 4.3.4 accepts every one of them and `fixed_pt_literal` (CORBA 3.4 §7.11.3) puts no such condition on the integer part. We follow omniidl and the grammar. `ZERO = 0.0d` and `ONE = 000000001d` are two of the values this file exists to keep — the first is the one a decimal type must be able to state at all, the second is the leading-zero normalisation `idl-diff` was measured against — so they stay, and the front end that cannot spell zero is what gets recorded.

column1: 33-const-values.idl
column4: CORBA 3.4 §7.11.1 makes `-2147483648` an ordinary `long` constant — it is the minimum of the type. omniidl 4.3.4 refuses it, and refuses `-9223372036854775808` as a `long long` the same way, because it types an integer literal by the *magnitude* it reads before applying the unary minus: 2147483648 does not fit a `long`, becomes `unsigned long`, and negating that is out of range. `short`'s minimum is unaffected — `-32768` folds through a `long` — which is what makes the pattern legible rather than arbitrary. Measured 2026-08-21 (M03, M05, M10; `-(2147483648)` fails identically, so it is the literal and not the spelling). We accept all three: a type whose minimum cannot be written is not the type the specification describes. The file carries `S_MIN` and deliberately not the other two, so it stays oracle-clean.

column1: 33-const-values.idl
column4: omniidl 4.3.4 reads a wide literal one *byte* at a time rather than one code point at a time. `L"a\u00e9b"` dumps back as three-plus code units with the two UTF-8 bytes of `\u00e9` as separate `\uffc3`/`\uffa9` escapes, and `L'\u00a7'` is not lexed at all — it reports "Error in look-up of 'L'", having decided the literal ended after one byte. Measured 2026-08-21. We decode wide literals as Unicode scalar values, which is what a `wchar` is (CORBA 3.4 §7.11.1) and what the codeset negotiation on the wire already assumes. `33-const-values.idl` and `30-const-type.idl` therefore keep their wide constants ASCII, so a golden file stays a file both front ends agree on; the non-ASCII code point is pinned in orbweaver-idl's unit tests instead.

column1: 33-const-values.idl
column4: `case_label ::= "case" const_exp ":"` and `const_exp` reaches `wide_character_literal`, so `union U switch (wchar) { case L'a': ... }` is legal by CORBA 3.4 §7.4.1.4.5. omniidl 4.3.4's union grammar does not admit a wide character literal in a case label and reports a syntax error (measured 2026-08-21, N03), though it takes the same literal in a `const`. We follow the grammar and accept it. No corpus file writes one — a golden file omniidl rejects is not a golden file — so the shape is pinned in orbweaver-idl's unit tests; this row exists so that the acceptance is recorded rather than discovered later as an unexplained laxity.

column1: n22-fixed-literal-shape.idl
column4: CORBA 3.4 §7.11.3 caps a `fixed` at 31 significant digits. omniidl 4.3.4 enforces that for the integer part — 32 integer digits is "Fixed point constant has too many digits" — and *silently truncates* the fractional part: `0.12345678901234567890123456789012d` (32 digits) dumps back as `0.1234567890123456789012345678901d`, one digit shorter than it was written, with no diagnostic. Measured 2026-08-21 (P13). We refuse both. Dropping a digit from a constant without saying so is precisely the failure this file's batch exists to close, and a value that is quietly not the one the author wrote is worse than a rejected file.

column1: n21-const-long-double.idl
column4: `const long double TOLERANCE = 1.0;`, and the same through a `typedef`, are refused by omniidl 4.3.4 ("Invalid type for constant: long double") and by us, and JacORB 3.9 compiles both with no diagnostic. What it writes is the measurement rather than the acceptance: `double value = 1.0;` — the constant becomes a Java `double`, and a `long double` silently becomes something narrower than it was declared, which is the outcome the refusal exists to prevent. Measured 2026-08-24. The grammar admits the type (`const_type` reaches `floating_pt_type`) and the refusal is semantic: there is no `long double` literal to write, so the declaration can never be completed with a value of its own type. We follow omniidl.
